shortQuestions: The Quraish army of about three thousand men marched to Madinah under Abu Sufyan; it included about seven hundred men in armour, two hundred horsemen and three thousand camels, with women who sang war songs to encourage the soldiers.

The Holy Prophet (ﷺ) suggested staying inside Madinah and defending it from within, because the city could be defended easily from its narrow streets and houses, the Muslims were far fewer than the enemy, and fighting in the open would be risky.

The young Companions, especially those who had missed Badr, were full of zeal and wanted to go out of the city and meet the enemy in the open battlefield; they felt that staying inside would look like weakness and cowardice.

He preferred the opinion of the youth because the majority favoured it and Islam teaches consultation (shura); he respected their enthusiasm and courage. Once the decision was made he put on his armour and did not go back on it.

At first the Muslims were winning and the Quraish fled. Seeing this, most of the fifty archers placed on the hill (Jabal al-Rumah) left their post to collect the spoils, against the Prophet's (ﷺ) order. Khalid bin Walid, then a commander of the Quraish cavalry, attacked from behind through the gap, and the battle turned against the Muslims.

When the infidels spread the false rumour that the Holy Prophet (ﷺ) had been martyred, many Muslims lost heart and some left the field, while others fought on bravely. When the Companions saw him alive, they gathered around him, protected him and took him to a safe place on the mountain; the Muslims regrouped and the Quraish withdrew.

The lesson is that obedience to the leader and discipline are essential for success; greed for worldly gain leads to disaster. It also teaches patience in hardship, unity, steadfastness and trust in Allah.

If the archers had not left the hill, Khalid's cavalry could not have attacked from behind; the Muslims would have completed their victory and the Quraish would have suffered a defeat like that of Badr.

At Badr (2 AH) 313 Muslims defeated a much larger Quraish army because of faith, obedience and Allah's help. Uhud (3 AH) was the Quraish's revenge for Badr; the Muslims began winning but suffered losses because of disobedience. Together they show that success comes with faith and obedience, and loss follows disobedience.
activities: Sample narration — The Battle of Uhud: Beginning — To take revenge for Badr, the Quraish marched on Madinah in 3 AH with about three thousand men. The Holy Prophet (ﷺ) consulted his Companions and, on the advice of the young men, went out to meet them near Mount Uhud with about seven hundred men after the hypocrites withdrew. He placed fifty archers on a hill with strict orders not to leave it. Middle — The Muslims attacked bravely and the Quraish fled. Seeing the spoils, most archers left the hill. Khalid bin Walid struck from behind; Hazrat Hamzah was martyred; the Prophet (ﷺ) was wounded and a rumour of his martyrdom spread. End — The Companions gathered round him and moved to the mountain; the Quraish went back without taking Madinah. The battle taught the Muslims the value of obedience and discipline.

Presentation guide: students read their narration of the Battle of Uhud to the class, using a clear beginning, middle and end, proper pronunciation and expression; classmates give feedback on organisation and language.
